issues.item: Triggers: Being Followed: Feeling followed or tracked
issues.explanation: 'Being followed or tracked' is difficult to reconcile with the stated trauma type of trauma to a loved one and with the rest of the profile, which centers on grief, guilt, and generalized somatic alarm rather than a pursuit/persecution context. It stands apart from the other trigger items and does not connect plausibly to the memory content provided.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy
issues.explanation: 'My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy' is not well aligned with the rest of the formulation and item set. The profile otherwise emphasizes guilt, grief, misery, fragmented/numb recall, and bodily false alarms after a loved-one trauma. A 'going crazy' appraisal is possible, but here it appears weakly supported by the trigger and memory content and feels clinically out of step relative to the otherwise bereavement/guilt-focused presentation.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Life Not Worth Living: I am not sure my life is worth living anymore
issues.explanation: For trauma to a loved one, severe guilt, misery, and a sense that life has been destroyed can be coherent. However, the specific appraisal 'I am not sure my life is worth living anymore' is notably more global and suicidal in tone than the rest of the selected profile, and it is not supported by corresponding threat, memory, trigger, or strategy content. With the provided five components, this item stands out as insufficiently anchored to the rest of the formulation-relevant material, making the node less internally coherent.

vignette:
Keoni was twenty-two when his younger brother, Ikaika, was killed by a drunk driver who ran a red light on a Friday night. Ikaika had been a passenger in his own car, waiting to turn left; the impact crushed the driver's side door. Keoni arrived at the hospital just after Ikaika was pronounced dead, and he saw the sheet pulled over his brother's face. The driver survived and later pleaded guilty to vehicular homicide, but at the sentencing the judge imposed only a two-year sentence, and Keoni felt the system had failed everyone he loved. In the months that followed, he could not string together a clear sequence of that night-the phone call, the drive, the waiting room lights all bled into one another, and whenever he tried to tell himself what happened, the story dissolved into fragments, leaving only a hollow sense that he had missed some chance to prevent it. Sometimes, when he did remember, he felt nothing at all, as though the scene had happened to a stranger, and that numbness shamed him even more than the guilt that usually came with recollection. Because the night of Ikaika's death existed only as fragments he could not hold together, Keoni began to feel that nearly anything could be a sign of disaster-the sharp click of a car door, the scent of hand sanitizer, a delay at the register-and he scanned every aisle for these cues before they could ambush him.

He worked as a pharmacist in a busy retail chain, and the job that once felt orderly now felt like a minefield. The smell of alcohol on a patient's breath-a common occurrence at the pharmacy counter-sent his heart racing before his mind could register why, and he would find himself gripping the counter, certain that something terrible was about to happen. He had begun to notice that his body reacted to danger before he had time to think; his muscles stayed tense all day, braced for a threat that never arrived, and more and more frequently he reacted as though he were in danger even when nothing was wrong. A customer who raised his voice about a prescription delay was enough to make Keoni's hands shake. He started to believe that his life had been destroyed by the trauma, that he used to be a happy person but now was always miserable, and that nothing in his life felt meaningful anymore. That conviction made him see threats everywhere: a customer's flat tone, a squeal of brakes on the street, even a patient complaining about wait times now felt like confirmations that the world was falling apart, and each of these became a fresh trigger for intrusive images of the hospital room. These thoughts sat at the core of everything: because he saw his future as empty, his body stayed on high alert, and that constant alarm only confirmed that he was broken, deepening his conviction that happiness was lost for good.

That belief-that his life was ruined-also shaped how his memory worked. When he was convinced that nothing mattered, the story of Ikaika's death felt even more disjointed, harder to hold onto, as if the tragedy belonged to someone else's life. And the heavier the guilt he carried, the more powerfully certain triggers yanked him back into that fragmented memory. The smell of alcohol, a funeral procession he saw from the pharmacy window, even a customer who cut in line and behaved rudely-these moments flooded him with half-formed images of the hospital room, and each intrusion reinforced his certainty that the driver's moral failure had stolen not just Ikaika but Keoni's entire sense of purpose.

Over the following year, avoidance became a quiet, daily habit. He stopped visiting the cemetery where Ikaika was buried because the sight of gravestones made his chest tighten and his memory fragment further. He asked to work only day shifts so he could avoid the evening customers who might have been drinking. He stopped attending family gatherings where people might talk about the accident. At work, he kept his head down and avoided engaging with any customer who complained or raised his voice, because those moments of moral violation-people misbehaving-triggered intrusive recollections of the driver's courtroom smirk. Each avoidance brought momentary relief, but it also narrowed his world. He began to feel trapped in a loop: a rude customer triggered his memory of the courtroom, which made him feel guilty and numb, which confirmed his appraisal that his life was over, which left his body tense and ready to react to the next trigger.

What finally brought him to a therapist was an incident at the pharmacy. A man came to pick up a prescription reeking of alcohol, and Keoni froze at the register, unable to speak. The man snapped at him to hurry up, and Keoni's hands shook so badly he dropped the vial. His manager pulled him aside afterward and asked if he was okay. Keoni said he was fine, but that night he could not sleep; he lay awake replaying the moment, the smell, the anger, and the thought that he was falling apart and could not stop it. He made an appointment the next morning because he was afraid that if he did not, he would lose his job-and then truly have nothing left. He was most afraid that talking about it would make the memories worse, but he was also desperate to feel even a small piece of the happiness he had once taken for granted.

violations.explanation: The vignette does not convey that memory influences or leads to triggers; instead, triggers repeatedly cause memory intrusions.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Memory → Triggers: The vignette does not convey that memory influences or leads to triggers; instead, triggers repeatedly cause memory intrusions.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
